GDP_LIVING_STANDARDS_LIMITS.label: Limits of GDP for living standards

stages.name: Limitations of GDP
stages.title: Limitations of GDP
stages.sub: After this the student can explain why a rising GDP figure does not always mean people are better off.

steps.q: Real GDP grows 5% and a newspaper says people must be better off. Does a bigger GDP always prove that?
steps.right: No, the figure can miss important things
steps.wrong: Yes, a bigger total always means better lives
steps.hint: GDP just totals up the market value of output. Could that total go up while something important about people's lives stays hidden?

steps.q: A parent looks after their children at home for free, and a neighbour grows vegetables to eat. Do these show up in GDP?
steps.right: No, unpaid and untraded work is left out
steps.wrong: Yes, GDP counts all useful work done
steps.hint: GDP is built from market transactions. Is any money changing hands for childcare done at home?

steps.q: Two countries have equal GDP per head, but only one shares income evenly. Does the GDP figure tell you which?
steps.right: No, the average hides how it is shared out
steps.wrong: Yes, an equal average means equal living standards
steps.hint: GDP per head is just a total divided by population. Does dividing by population tell you who actually holds the money?

steps.q: A factory's output raises GDP, but its smoke pollutes the local river and air. Does the GDP figure subtract anything for that pollution?
steps.right: No, the damage is not subtracted
steps.wrong: Yes, GDP falls to reflect the pollution
steps.hint: GDP adds up the value of what is produced and sold. Is the cost of harm done to the environment part of that sale price?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: One country spends its GDP on hospitals and leisure, another on weapons and long hours. Does the total tell them apart?
steps.right: No, the total looks the same either way
steps.wrong: Yes, a higher-wellbeing mix shows a higher GDP
steps.hint: GDP just adds up the value of output, whatever that output actually is. Does it say what the output was for?
